sentences.pattern: Equal treatment produces equal opportunity only when + starting conditions + are comparable.
sentences.cn: 只有起点条件相当时，同等对待才会带来机会平等。
sentences.example: Equal treatment produces equal opportunity only when applicants face comparable barriers.

sentences.pattern: Removing + formal barrier + does not automatically eliminate + informal disadvantage.
sentences.cn: 消除正式障碍并不会自动消除非正式劣势。
sentences.example: Removing an application fee does not automatically eliminate unequal access to guidance.

sentences.pattern: The extent to which + selection method + is fair depends on whether it measures + relevant ability.
sentences.cn: 某选拔方法是否公平，取决于它是否衡量相关能力。
sentences.example: The extent to which an interview is fair depends on whether it measures skills needed for the role.

writingIdeas.viewpoint: Fair selection should measure relevant capability directly.
writingIdeas.topicSentence: Recruitment and admission become more equitable when evidence is closely connected to the task.
writingIdeas.argument: Informal interviews can reward shared background, confidence or familiarity with unwritten conventions. A structured work sample gives candidates the same task and criteria, producing evidence closer to future performance. Adjustments may still be needed so disability or equipment does not distort the result. No method removes judgement entirely, but explicit criteria make decisions easier to challenge and improve. Merit is more credible when the process reveals what it actually means.

writingIdeas.topicSentence: Providing the same resource to everyone can preserve disadvantage when starting barriers differ.
writingIdeas.argument: A free course is formally open, yet a learner without transport, childcare or a device may remain unable to attend. Targeted grants or equipment do not guarantee success; they reduce an obstacle unrelated to academic effort. Support should be proportionate and reviewed for effectiveness. Treating every difference in provision as unfair confuses identical inputs with meaningful access. Equal opportunity concerns the ability to participate and demonstrate competence, not the appearance of uniform treatment.

speaking.question: Do you think people have equal educational opportunities?
speaking.answer: No, even where schools are free, resources and conditions differ. Some pupils have quiet space, tutoring and informed advice, while others manage work or care responsibilities. Schools can reduce these gaps, but they cannot control every household factor. Equality needs to be examined in practical access, not only formal rules.

speaking.question: Describe a situation in which someone was given a fair opportunity.
speaking.answer: I saw a fair process when a community organisation recruited assistants for an event. Instead of asking for previous event experience, it gave applicants a short scheduling problem and clear information about the role. Interviews used the same questions, and candidates could request an accessible format. One successful applicant had never worked at an event but showed excellent organisation through caring responsibilities and school projects. Training covered the specific procedures afterwards. The process seemed fair because it did not lower the standard; it measured the abilities actually needed and allowed different backgrounds to provide evidence. It also showed how an entry-level opportunity can remain genuinely open to beginners.

reading.title: The Audition Behind a Screen
paragraphs: Orchestras have used screened auditions to reduce the influence of identity on selection. Musicians perform behind a barrier so judges hear without seeing name, gender or appearance. The method is often cited as proof that removing information produces merit-based choice. Its effect, however, depends on which stage of opportunity is examined.

A screen can reduce visual bias during performance, but it cannot equalise years of access to instruments, tuition and time for practice. Travel costs may affect who attends, while reputation can influence earlier shortlisting if recordings are not anonymous. Fairness at one decision point does not erase unequal preparation or entry.

The method also works because musical performance can be sampled directly. In occupations where collaboration, explanation or physical interaction matters, complete anonymity may remove relevant evidence. The appropriate lesson is not that every selection process should be blind, but that irrelevant information should be separated from the capability being assessed wherever possible.

Procedural details matter. Footsteps can reveal footwear, judges may recognise a distinctive style and the order of performance can affect attention. Organisations refine screens, carpets and scoring criteria in response. These imperfections do not make the attempt useless; they show that fairness is a design problem requiring testing rather than a one-time declaration.

A fair opportunity has several stages: preparation, entry, assessment and progression. Intervention at one stage can produce meaningful improvement while leaving other barriers in place. Claims should therefore be precise. A screened audition can make one judgement more focused on sound, but equality requires continued attention to who reaches the screen and what happens after selection. Progression is frequently the least visible stage. An organisation may recruit a diverse entry group while promotion relies on informal sponsorship and assignments offered through existing networks. Publishing criteria, tracking access to developmental work and reviewing who advances can reveal where opportunity narrows later. Fair entry is meaningful, but it should open a pathway rather than produce a diverse first photograph.
